THOUGHT: This young woman is 12 weeks post–right tympanoplasty via a likely postauricular approach and has improved hearing but now reports intermittent lancinating ear pain with chewing and pain/pressure sensitivity when wearing earrings. Key findings: no fever, normal vitals, no TMJ click or mandibular tenderness (makes primary TMJ disorder less likely), audiology improved (no recurrent middle-ear infection), and the pain is mechanically triggered (eating, pressure from earrings). Differential includes trigeminal neuralgia (V3/auriculotemporal) or glossopharyngeal neuralgia, persistent/recurrent infection or mastoiditis (no systemic signs), referred otalgia from TMJ (exam not supportive), and post‑surgical neuropathic pain from injured sensory nerves to the auricle. Tympanoplasty with a postauricular incision commonly risks injury to sensory branches (greater auricular nerve and/or auriculotemporal fibers) producing neuropathic otalgia and hypersensitivity of the external ear and earlobe (explaining pain with earrings). Chewing can provoke pain by movement of soft tissues and parotid region innervated by auriculotemporal/greater auricular pathways, producing shooting pains. The absence of objective jaw findings and lack of red flags (neurologic deficits, progressive focal signs) make central causes like brainstem lesion or classic trigeminal/glossopharyngeal neuralgia less likely. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is post‑tympanoplasty neuropathic otalgia from injury/irritation of the auricular sensory nerves (postoperative auricular neuralgia, e.g., greater auricular/auriculotemporal nerve neuropathy).

DIAGNOSIS: Post‑tympanoplasty neuropathic otalgia — postoperative auricular neuralgia (likely greater auricular/auriculotemporal nerve injury).

ANALYSIS: The prediction proposes a postoperative peripheral auricular neuropathy (greater auricular/auriculotemporal) related to the postauricular incision—consistent with pain triggered by local pressure (earrings) after tympanoplasty. The reference is glossopharyngeal neuralgia, a distinct cranial nerve IX pain syndrome classically triggered by swallowing, coughing or throat stimulation and producing paroxysmal lancinating pain in the pharynx/tonsillar area and sometimes referred otalgia. The predicted diagnosis does not identify glossopharyngeal neuralgia and instead attributes symptoms to local surgical nerve injury; these are different entities.
